FrugalEvo: Towards Cost-Aware LLM-Guided Program Evolution

Hui Chen ††thanks: Correspondence to: hui.chen@nus.edu.sg Affiliation:  National University of Singapore    Xuan Qi Affiliation:  University of Washington    James Xu Zhao Affiliation:  National University of Singapore    Zhaopeng Feng Affiliation:  National University of Singapore    Shilong Liu Affiliation:  Princeton University    Kuang Xu   Pang Wei Koh   Bryan Hooi Affiliation:  National University of Singapore Affiliation:  University of Washington Affiliation:  Stanford University[0.25em] Code: https://github.com/chchenhui/frugalevo
Abstract

LLM-guided evolutionary methods, such as AlphaEvolve, have emerged as powerful approaches for challenging computational optimization problems, such as circle packing. However, prior work typically optimizes performance gain over a fixed number of iterations. We argue that practical optimization should maximize gain per unit cost. To this end, we propose FrugalEvo, a cost-aware evolutionary framework where a stronger, higher-cost LLM explores solution strategies, and a cheaper LLM implements them and iteratively refines the resulting code. We also design a cache-efficient evolution process, where our harness and prompts maximize the sharing of prefixes across different evolution steps, to improve cache reuse. To measure solution quality throughout a fixed cost budget, we introduce Budget-Aware Area Under the Curve (BA-AUC), defined as the area under the best-so-far evaluation score curve over cumulative LLM cost, up to the budget. Across 10 mathematical and systems optimization tasks, FrugalEvo matches or surpasses state-of-the-art baselines, including OpenEvolve, ShinkaEvolve, AdaEvolve, and EvoX, in final solution quality and achieves higher BA-AUC on 9 tasks. It also achieves higher average performance than these baselines on 10 algorithmic optimization tasks from ALE-Bench-Lite. Notably, on circle packing, FrugalEvo achieves new state-of-the-art performance with GPT-5.6 Terra and Luna for only $1.68 and with GLM-5.3 and its Flash variant for only $0.55, matching or surpassing all baselines, including multi-agent methods such as CORAL and SwarmResearch, which cost approximately $50 on average.

1 Introduction

Rapid advances in large language models (LLMs) have accelerated scientific discovery across diverse domains (Feng et al., 2026b; Liu et al., 2026a; Wang et al., 2026). In particular, LLM-guided evolutionary methods, such as AlphaEvolve (Novikov et al., 2025), OpenEvolve (Sharma, 2025), and ShinkaEvolve (Lange et al., 2026), have shown promise in computational optimization problems, including mathematics (Glazer et al., 2024), systems (Cheng et al., 2025), and algorithmic optimization (Imajuku et al., 2026). These methods typically maintain a pool of high-performing programs or solutions; they iteratively select a parent from this pool, prompt an LLM to propose a mutation, and then evaluate the resulting candidate. Progress is often measured as performance after a given number of evolutionary iterations (Liu et al., 2026b; Cemri et al., 2026), with curves plotted against the number of LLM-generated candidates or evaluator calls.

However, focusing on performance after a fixed number of iterations may overlook a key practical constraint in computational optimization: the total cost. This cost may include API fees or GPU compute costs for LLM inference, CPU compute costs for evaluator execution, and other CPU/GPU resource costs associated with task execution. On many challenging tasks, AI agents achieve better performance with more inference-time computation, a phenomenon known as test-time scaling (Snell et al., 2024; Brown et al., 2024; Muennighoff et al., 2025). Consequently, higher performance alone does not establish greater efficiency, as it may simply reflect higher expenditure. We therefore argue that methods should be assessed by their performance-cost trade-offs and their ability to maximize solution quality under a fixed cost budget. This shifts the focus from gain per iteration to gain per unit cost. To measure gain per unit cost, we introduce a new metric, Budget-Aware Area Under the Curve (BA-AUC), based on the performance achieved at each cost budget.

Next, we propose FrugalEvo, a cost-aware LLM-guided evolutionary framework for computational optimization. Since LLM inference often accounts for the largest proportion of search costs in this domain, compared with those of evaluator execution and other CPU/GPU operations, we focus on improving the cost efficiency of LLM inference. As shown in Figure 1(a), FrugalEvo splits candidate program generation into two steps and uses two different models to carry them out: a strong, high-cost LLM explores diverse, promising design strategies, while a weaker, low-cost LLM implements them as executable programs and iteratively refines the resulting code.

Beyond model collaboration, we design a cache-efficient evolution process for FrugalEvo. Inference systems and APIs that support prompt caching can reuse cached key-value (KV) states for identical prompt prefixes, reducing latency and cost. To facilitate this reuse, we design our harness and prompts to maximize the sharing of prefixes across different evolution steps, improving cache reuse.

We evaluate FrugalEvo on 20 tasks spanning mathematical, systems, and algorithmic optimization (Section 3). With two model configurations—GPT-5.6 Terra and Luna (OpenAI, 2026), and GLM-5.3 and its Flash variant (Z.ai, 2026b; Z.ai, 2026a)—FrugalEvo matches or outperforms OpenEvolve (Sharma, 2025), ShinkaEvolve (Lange et al., 2026), AdaEvolve (Cemri et al., 2026), and EvoX (Liu et al., 2026b) in final solution quality and BA-AUC on 9 of 10 mathematical and systems optimization tasks. It also achieves the highest average performance across 10 algorithmic optimization tasks and matches or surpasses the reported AlphaEvolve (Novikov et al., 2025) results on all four mathematical tasks with available comparisons. Notably, as shown in Figure 1(b), FrugalEvo achieves a sum of radii of 2.63599 on Circle Packing using GLM-5.3 and its Flash variant for only $0.55, surpassing all baselines, including multi-agent methods which cost approximately $50 on average. Moreover, Figure 1(c) shows that FrugalEvo substantially reduces the average cost per iteration.

In summary, our contributions include:

  • •

    We argue that practical LLM-guided evolutionary search in computational optimization should focus on improving performance gain per unit cost. In this work, we introduce Budget-Aware Area Under the Curve (BA-AUC) to assess solution quality throughout a fixed LLM cost budget, complementing evaluation based on final scores.

  • •

    We propose FrugalEvo, a cost-aware evolutionary framework that combines strategy exploration by a strong, high-cost model with code implementation and refinement by a low-cost model, and design a cache-efficient evolution process.

  • •

    We evaluate FrugalEvo on 20 real-world computational optimization tasks. FrugalEvo matches or surpasses all baselines, including OpenEvolve, ShinkaEvolve, AdaEvolve, and EvoX, in solution quality and achieves higher BA-AUC on 9 of 10 mathematical and systems optimization tasks. It also achieves the highest average performance on 10 algorithmic optimization tasks.

2 FrugalEvo: Cost-Aware Program Evolution

2.1 Problem Formulation

Following prior work (Novikov et al., 2025; Romera-Paredes et al., 2024), we formulate LLM-guided evolutionary search as a program optimization process under a fixed budget.

Candidate Evaluation.

Let 𝒳\mathcal{X} denote the program space and let x0∈𝒳x_{0}\in\mathcal{X} be an initial program, which is an example given by the task. An evaluator evaluates each candidate x∈𝒳x\in\mathcal{X} and returns a task-specific score and auxiliary feedback:

E⁡(x)=(s⁡(x),a⁡(x)),E:𝒳→ℝ×𝒜,E(x)=(s(x),a(x)),\qquad E:\mathcal{X}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}\times\mathcal{A}, (1)

where s⁡(x)∈ℝs(x)\in\mathbb{R} is the task-specific score to be maximized and a⁡(x)∈𝒜a(x)\in\mathcal{A} contains auxiliary feedback.

Program Database and Search Context.

Evaluated programs and their results are stored in a program database. Evaluating the initial program x0x_{0} initializes the database as 𝒟0={(x0,s0,a0)}\mathcal{D}_{0}=\{(x_{0},s_{0},a_{0})\}. At iteration tt, a search strategy SS constructs a search context CS​(𝒟t)C_{S}(\mathcal{D}_{t}) by combining the task description and analysis with a parent program, sampled reference programs, their evaluation results, and summaries of previous attempts retrieved from 𝒟t\mathcal{D}_{t}. Conditioned on this context, an LLM GLLMG_{\mathrm{LLM}} generates a new candidate, which is then evaluated:

xt+1∼GLLM(⋅∣CS(𝒟t)),E(xt+1)=(st+1,at+1).x_{t+1}\sim G_{\mathrm{LLM}}\!\left(\cdot\mid C_{S}(\mathcal{D}_{t})\right),\qquad E(x_{t+1})=(s_{t+1},a_{t+1}). (2)

The resulting record is added to the database as 𝒟t+1=𝒟t∪{(xt+1,st+1,at+1)}\mathcal{D}_{t+1}=\mathcal{D}_{t}\cup\{(x_{t+1},s_{t+1},a_{t+1})\}.

Optimization Goal.

As cost is a key factor in determining the practical utility of an approach, we focus on maximizing solution quality

s⋆=max(x,s,a)∈𝒟B⁡ss^{\star}=\max_{(x,s,a)\in\mathcal{D}_{B}}s (3)

under a fixed cost budget BB.

Budget-Aware AUC.

We introduce Budget-Aware Area Under the Curve (BA-AUC) to measure how efficiently a method improves solution quality within a fixed LLM cost budget. Let q⁡(c)q(c) denote the best-so-far evaluation score at cumulative LLM cost cc. For a fixed cost budget BB, we define

BA​-​AUC⁡(B)=∫0Bq⁡(c)​𝑑c.\operatorname{BA\text{-}AUC}(B)=\int_{0}^{B}q(c)\,\mathrm{d}c. (4)

To compare all methods over the same cost interval [0,B][0,B], we hold the best-so-far evaluation score constant up to BB if a run ends before reaching the budget, and truncate the curve at BB if the run exceeds it.

2.2 Our Approach

Overview.

Figure 2 presents an overview of our approach, which proceeds as follows: (1) starting from an initial program, the cold start module establishes an “incumbent”—the best-performing program found so far—as the parent code for strategy exploration and solution generation; (2) the context builder combines the problem context, task analysis, and incumbent program with information from search memory; (3) the strategy explorer uses a high-cost LLM to propose multiple design strategies; (4) the solution generator uses a low-cost LLM to implement and refine the proposed strategies; (5) the search memory updates the search context for the next round of strategy exploration; and (6) the process repeats until the budget is exhausted, returning the best program found. A detailed algorithm description is provided in Appendix A and prompts of strategy explorer and solution generator can be found in Appendix D.

Cold Start.

The strategy explorer generates design strategies based on a parent program. Using a weak initial program as the parent may lead to low-quality strategies and inefficient use of the cost budget. We therefore introduce a cold-start phase in which a low-cost LLM iteratively refines the initial program until the evaluation score no longer improves. The best resulting program becomes the initial incumbent and serves as the parent for the first round of strategy exploration.

Context Builder.

The context builder organizes task information and search history to guide strategy exploration. At the start of evolution, the context builder uses a high-cost LLM to analyze the problem description and evaluator code to identify the optimization objective and evaluation constraints. It combines this information with the incumbent program established by cold start and its evaluation feedback to construct the initial search context. As the search progresses, it updates the context with the latest incumbent and attempted programs, strategies, and evaluation feedback retrieved from the search memory, guiding subsequent strategy exploration.

Cache-Efficient Prompt Construction.

Specifically, to reduce input-token costs, we construct cache-efficient prompts by placing shared content at the beginning, enabling prefix reuse through API prompt caching.11 1 A couple of LLM API providers support prompt caching, allowing repeated prompt prefixes to be reused at a lower input-token cost; e.g., OpenAI: https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/prompt-caching. To maximize prefix reuse between attempts, each prompt begins with fixed content (task instructions, output requirements, etc.). This is followed by information which changes less frequently, e.g., contextual examples, with island-best and elite programs appearing first before randomly sampled programs, lastly followed by frequently changing information, preserving the maximum amount of shared prefix across successive attempts. Additionally, feedback from each attempt is appended to the end of the prompt, allowing cache usage.

Strategy Explorer.

Since algorithmic design can substantially affect solution quality, we use a strong, high-cost LLM to explore diverse design strategies. Given the search context, including the parent program, evaluation feedback, and previously explored strategies, it proposes multiple distinct strategies in a single API call. Each strategy provides a concrete plan for modifying the parent program, explaining what to change, why it may improve performance, and what computational limits to follow. The proposed strategies are then passed to the solution generator for implementation and refinement.

Solution Generator.

The solution generator uses a low-cost LLM to implement and refine the proposed strategies. It first generates one trial implementation per strategy and ranks the strategies by their evaluation scores. It then follows this ranking to select strategies for further refinement. Each refinement round fixes one strategy and the current incumbent as the parent program, allowing up to MM sequential implementation attempts. Each attempt is evaluated, and feedback from unsuccessful attempts informs subsequent prompts while the parent remains unchanged. As soon as an attempt improves the incumbent, the round ends, the improved program becomes the new incumbent, and another round begins with the same strategy and the updated parent. If a round ends without improvement, the generator moves to the next strategy.

Evaluator and Search Memory.

The evaluator assesses each generated candidate program using task-specific scoring functions. Search memory uses island-based MAP-Elites (Mouret and Clune, 2015; Tanese, 1989) to maintain program diversity. It stores candidate programs and their evaluation results, along with proposed strategies, the results of strategy attempts, and failure feedback. The evolution process stops when the remaining budget cannot cover further LLM calls and returns the best program found.

3 Experiments

3.1 Experimental Setup

Tasks.

We evaluate FrugalEvo on 20 real-world optimization tasks, including 5 mathematics optimization problems (Sharma, 2025), 5 systems optimization tasks from the ADRS benchmark (Cheng et al., 2025), and 10 algorithmic optimization problems from ALE-Bench-Lite (Imajuku et al., 2026). Benchmark details are provided in Appendix B.

Baselines.

We compare FrugalEvo against strong LLM-guided evolutionary methods, including OpenEvolve (Sharma, 2025), ShinkaEvolve (Lange et al., 2026), AdaEvolve (Cemri et al., 2026), and EvoX (Liu et al., 2026b). For mathematical tasks, we additionally report state-of-the-art results from AlphaEvolve (Novikov et al., 2025).

Model Configurations and Budget.

We use two model configurations in our evaluation. In the first configuration, FrugalEvo uses GPT-5.6 Terra (OpenAI, 2026) for strategy generation and GPT-5.6 Luna (OpenAI, 2026) for code implementation and refinement, while all four baselines use GPT-5.6 Terra. Each run receives an LLM cost budget of $2 per run for mathematical optimization tasks and $1 for systems and algorithmic optimization tasks. In the second configuration, FrugalEvo uses GLM-5.3 (Z.ai, 2026b) for strategy generation and GLM-5.3 Flash (Z.ai, 2026a) for implementation and refinement, while other baselines use GLM-5.3. The corresponding budgets are $1 for mathematical tasks and $0.5 for systems optimization tasks. Model Pricing details are provided in Appendix C.

3.2 Main Results

Results on Math Optimization Tasks.

We evaluate five tasks spanning geometric packing, extremal geometry, distance-ratio minimization, and multi-objective signal filtering. As shown in Table 1, FrugalEvo achieves the highest mean BA-AUC on all five tasks under both model configurations. It also achieves the best or comparable mean performance on all five tasks using GPT-5.6 Terra and Luna and four using GLM-5.3 and the Flash variant. Compared to the strong reported results in the closed-source AlphaEvolve, FrugalEvo matches or exceeds AlphaEvolve on four tasks, including Circle Packing, Heilbronn Convex (13), Heilbronn Triangle, and Min-Max-3.

Solution Analysis.

Beyond aggregate scores, FrugalEvo discovers qualitatively distinct solutions across different tasks. On Circle Packing, it finds a packing with a total radius of 2.635996 by evolving five-row layouts with asymmetric displacements, refining them through constrained SLSQP optimization and fixed-center radius linear programming, and applying small radius increases within the evaluator’s tolerance.

Figure 3 visualizes the solutions discovered by FrugalEvo and compares them with the initial program on Circle Packing. It shows that FrugalEvo improves the sum of radii on Circle Packing from 0.95976 to 2.635996 using GPT-5.6 Terra and Luna for $1.68, and to 2.635990 using GLM-5.3 and its Flash variant for $0.55. These results are better than or comparable to those of CORAL (Qu et al., 2026) and SwarmResearch (Virk et al., 2026), which cost approximately $50 on average to achieve 2.635985 and 2.635996, respectively, demonstrating substantial cost savings.

Moreover, on Signal Processing, FrugalEvo reaches 0.78912 by adaptively blending Savitzky–Golay, Butterworth, and spectral filters while suppressing minor reversals. On Heilbronn Convex (13), FrugalEvo matches AlphaEvolve through multistart hill climbing, linear programming refinement, and convex-hull area reduction. These results indicate the effectiveness of our approach: using a stronger model to explore strategies and a weaker model to iteratively refine solutions.

Results on Systems Optimization Tasks.

Table 2 reports results on five real-world systems optimization tasks from the ADRS benchmark (Cheng et al., 2025). It shows that FrugalEvo achieves the best or comparable mean and best performance on all five tasks under both model configurations, with the highest mean BA-AUC on four tasks.

Qualitatively, FrugalEvo discovers effective approaches to systems optimization. On EPLB, it achieves a score of 0.1473 with an expert load-balancing algorithm that combines greedy expert replication, load-aware block assignment, and pairwise swap refinement. On Transaction Scheduling, it achieves a combined score of 4405.29 with a scheduler that combines multistart regret-guided insertion, exhaustive local window reordering, and transaction relocation to reduce makespan.

Results on Algorithmic Optimization Tasks.

We evaluate FrugalEvo on 10 algorithmic optimization tasks from ALE-Bench-Lite (Imajuku et al., 2026), derived from AtCoder Heuristic Contests, and report the results in Figure 4. Following prior work (Lange et al., 2026), all methods start from solutions produced by ALE-Agent (Imajuku et al., 2026) and are evaluated using private scores.

As shown in Figure 4, FrugalEvo achieves the highest score of 1924.9, outperforming strong baselines OpenEvolve (1887.5) and AdaEvolve (1881.9). It discovers diverse algorithmic optimization solutions. On AHC016 (graph classification), FrugalEvo constructs graphs from disjoint cliques and their complements, identifying noisy graphs by comparing the sorted numbers of neighbors per vertex with noise-adjusted expectations. On AHC027 (cleaning route), FrugalEvo uses dirt accumulation rates, time since the last visit, and travel distances to plan routes that revisit areas requiring more frequent cleaning.

Performance-For-Cost Curves.

To compare cost efficiency, we plot performance-for-cost curves of different methods on Signal Processing, Heilbronn Convex (13), and Transaction Scheduling. As shown in Figure 5, FrugalEvo establishes a clear performance advantage within the first $0.2 on all three tasks and maintains it throughout the remaining search. Its higher mean BA-AUC values on all three tasks further quantify this advantage over the cost interval. These results indicate that FrugalEvo achieves higher search efficiency within a given cost budget.

3.3 Ablations

In this section, we present ablation studies on key components of FrugalEvo (model collaboration, cold start, and sequential feedback in code refinement) and the results are shown in Table 3.

Impact of Model Collaboration.

Our framework assigns strategy exploration and solution generation to different models to improve search efficiency. As shown in Table 3, using either the high-cost or low-cost model for both stages yields lower mean and best performance than FrugalEvo on both tasks under the same cost budget. In particular, using only the high-cost model leads to a larger drop in mean performance, possibly because implementation calls consume a substantial portion of the budget, leaving less for further exploration. Moreover, using only the low-cost model reduces the best final score, particularly on Signal Processing. This may be because the low-cost model is less effective at identifying promising strategies. These results suggest that combining strategy exploration by a strong, expensive model with low-cost code implementation improves search efficiency under a fixed cost budget.

Impact of Cold Start and Sequential Feedback.

We introduce a cold-start phase to provide a stronger initial incumbent for strategy exploration. As shown in Table 3, removing this phase and using the initial program directly as the parent reduces both mean and best performance on both tasks. This suggests that refining the initial program with a low-cost model is a cost-effective way to support high-quality strategy exploration. Moreover, we also incorporate sequential feedback into code refinement in the solution generator. Removing this feedback lowers mean performance and increases the standard deviation across runs, suggesting that feedback from earlier attempts helps the low-cost model refine programs more effectively and improves search stability.

4 Related Work

LLM-Guided Evolutionary Methods.

Recent work combining LLMs with evolutionary search has produced notable results (Agrawal et al., 2026; Novikov et al., 2025) for mathematical (Feng et al., 2026c; Feng et al., 2026d; Feng et al., 2026b), algorithmic (Mang et al., 2025), and systems (Cheng et al., 2025) optimization. For example, FunSearch (Romera-Paredes et al., 2024) combines LLM generation with automated evaluation to evolve mathematical solutions. AlphaEvolve (Novikov et al., 2025) extends this approach from evolving individual functions to larger programs. Subsequently, OpenEvolve (Sharma, 2025) and CodeEvolve (Assumpção et al., 2025) provide open-source frameworks, and ShinkaEvolve (Lange et al., 2026) introduces a sample-efficient evolution method. ThetaEvolve (Wang et al., 2025) and TTT-Discover (Yuksekgonul et al., 2026) apply Reinforcement Learning (RL) to improve the LLM generator at test time. More recently, AdaEvolve (Cemri et al., 2026) and EvoX (Liu et al., 2026b) adapt the search process, while SwarmResearch (Virk et al., 2026) and CORAL (Qu et al., 2026) coordinate multiple coding agents to improve search performance. These methods focus on performance gains over a fixed number of iterations, while our work emphasizes gain per unit cost.

Cost-Efficient LLM Inference.

Prior work explores LLM cascades (Chen et al., 2023), routing (Ong et al., 2025; Feng et al., 2026a), reflection (Agrawal et al., 2026; Zhang et al., 2026a), and caching (Zhang et al., 2026b) to improve cost efficiency. For instance, FrugalGPT (Chen et al., 2023) learns model cascades to balance cost and accuracy, while RouteLLM (Ong et al., 2025) learns to route queries between strong and weak models using preference data. For scientific discovery, SimpleTES (Ye et al., 2026) post-trains an open-source model for long-horizon AI discovery by assigning each attempt the final outcome of the trajectory it helped produce. Meanwhile, Squeeze Evolve (Maheswaran et al., 2026) coordinates multiple models for verifier-free evolution using models’ own confidence signals, such as token log-probabilities. Our approach allocates model capability based on the characteristics of computational optimization tasks, without additional model training or access to token-level probabilities.

5 Conclusion

We introduce FrugalEvo, a cost-aware LLM-guided evolutionary framework for computational optimization, that combines strategy exploration by a strong, high-cost model with code implementation and refinement by a low-cost model, and design a cache-efficient evolution process. To assess solution quality throughout a fixed cost budget, we propose Budget-Aware Area Under the Curve (BA-AUC). Across diverse real-world computational optimization tasks, FrugalEvo matches or surpasses all baselines in solution quality and achieves higher BA-AUC on the majority of tasks.

Limitations and Future Work.

FrugalEvo splits candidate program generation in computational optimization tasks into two steps and assigns them to two different models. This design is tailored to settings where both solution generation and evaluation take place entirely within a code environment, so that candidates can be executed and scored automatically. As a result, our method does not readily extend to scientific domains that require interaction with the physical world, such as biology, where evaluating a solution may involve wet-lab experiments that cannot be automated through code execution. Moreover, guiding the model to explore effective strategies relies on carefully crafted instructions. Our current instructions are manually designed for computational optimization tasks rather than automatically derived from each task. Finally, future work includes extending this approach to other domains that require interaction with the physical world, and develop methods that automatically generate strategy exploration instructions.

AI Use Statement

In preparing this submission, we used LLMs as general-purpose writing assistants and coding agents to implement the algorithm and run experiments. The human authors were responsible for the entire research process, including initial ideation, experimental design, and data analysis. For the experiments, the authors first developed an experimental plan and prepared the codebase and datasets, then instructed coding agents to implement the proposed method and execute the experiments. During writing, the authors drafted each section, including all core ideas and technical details, and used LLMs to improve clarity, coherence, and grammar. All scientific claims and findings presented in this paper originate from the authors, who take full responsibility for the final content.

Ethics Statement

Our work adheres to the ICLR Code of Ethics. The primary ethical considerations for this research involve the use of solutions generated by our algorithm across 20 optimization tasks. Although assessed by task evaluators, these solutions have not been validated by human experts and are intended for research reference only.

Reproducibility Statement

We are committed to ensuring the reproducibility of our research. To this end, we will publicly release all code, data, and supplementary materials upon publication.
